lesson.title: Blocking the Rumble: How High-Pass Filters Work
lesson.summary: A high-pass filter passes frequencies above its cutoff frequency largely unattenuated and increasingly suppresses frequencies below it, the mirror image of a low-pass filter built by simply swapping the resistor and capacitor positions.
lesson.body:
A high-pass filter, also a member of the family introduced in Filter, does the opposite job of a low-pass filter: its passband is above the cutoff frequency and its stopband is below it. It shares the same cutoff frequency definition from Cutoff Frequency, the point where output has fallen to 0.707 of input, about minus 3 dB.

The simplest high-pass filter takes the low-pass RC divider and swaps the two components' roles: the capacitor goes in series with the signal, and the resistor connects the output node to ground. At low frequencies the capacitor's reactance is large, so most of the input voltage is dropped across the capacitor itself and very little reaches the resistor, meaning the output is small. At high frequencies the capacitor's reactance shrinks toward zero, so it behaves like a short circuit, passing the signal through to the resistor with little loss. Same two components as the low-pass filter, opposite arrangement, opposite frequency behavior.

The cutoff frequency formula is identical in form to the low-pass case, fc = 1/(2πRC), because it depends only on the RC time constant, not on which component is in series and which is shunt.

Take R = 4.7 kΩ and C = 33 nF. RC = 4700 times 33 times 10 to the minus 9, which is 1.551 times 10 to the minus 4 seconds. fc = 1/(2π times 1.551 times 10 to the minus 4), about 1026 Hz, roughly 1.03 kHz. Below about 1.03 kHz this filter attenuates the signal, above it, the signal passes through largely intact.

A common everyday use is blocking low-frequency rumble or a DC offset from an audio signal while letting the frequencies you actually want to hear pass through unimpeded. Like the low-pass filter, this circuit has only one reactive element, so it too is a first-order filter, and its attenuation below cutoff grows at 20 dB per decade as frequency drops further from fc, exactly the roll-off rate covered in Roll-Off Rate.
